analogy.p: Starch is a key and the amylase active site is a lock. At the optimum pH the lock is the perfect shape, so keys turn quickly and many starch molecules are broken down each second. Wrong pH is like damp warping the lock: the key no longer fits and nothing happens. Iodine is a guard that checks whether any uncut keys are left. Where it breaks down: a real active site is not rigid, and denaturing changes the bonds holding the enzyme's shape, not just squashing it.
analogy.t: Lock and key in a warped door

bullets: A **qualitative test** gives a yes/no result from a colour change or appearance. It tells you whether a substance is present, not how much (although the Benedict's colour scale gives a rough idea).
The four food tests you must know: **iodine** (starch), **Benedict's** (sugars), **biuret** (protein) and **ethanol emulsion** (lipids).
The enzyme practical is a **quantitative** investigation: you measure the time taken for the reaction to finish and convert it to a **rate**.
Exam questions are often worth 4 to 6 marks and ask you to **describe a method**, so learn the steps in order with the quantities and conditions.
You also need maths skills: calculating a rate as 1/time, plotting a line graph, finding the optimum from a curve and calculating a mean.
The practical links directly to **digestive enzymes** (4.2.2), the **lock and key model** and the effects of temperature and pH on enzymes.
core.h: What the specification asks you to do
core.p: This spec point covers two linked required practicals. First, you must be able to use **qualitative reagents** to test for a range of **carbohydrates, lipids and proteins**. Second, you must investigate the **effect of pH on the rate of reaction of the enzyme amylase**, using the iodine test for starch to tell you when the reaction is finished. Both are tested in the exam as method questions, as data and graph questions, and as 'evaluate the investigation' questions, so you need to know the procedures, the colour changes, the hazards and the reasons behind each step.

bullets: **Break up** the food using a **pestle and mortar** (or a mixer or knife) so that more surface area is exposed.
Add a small volume of **distilled water** and grind or stir to form a paste or suspension. Distilled water is used because tap water contains dissolved substances that could affect the test.
**Filter** the mixture (filter paper and funnel) to remove solid pieces. The clear filtrate is the **food solution** used for the tests.
Use the **same volume of food solution** (for example 2 cm3) in each test tube so that colour changes can be compared.
Label each test tube with a **marker pen** so you know which food is which.
A **control** tube containing distilled water and the reagent shows the negative result or starting colour for comparison.
If you are testing a liquid food such as milk, no grinding or filtering is needed.
core.h: Preparing a food sample for testing
core.p: Food tests only work reliably if the food molecules can mix with the test reagent, so the food must be turned into a liquid sample first. This is why solid foods are broken up before any reagent is added. Good preparation also removes solid lumps and coloured pieces that would hide a colour change, which makes the result easier to judge and fairer to compare between foods.

bullets: Place about **2 cm3 of the food solution** in a test tube (or put a drop of the food on a spotting tile).
Add a few **drops of iodine solution** and gently shake or stir.
**Positive result**: the iodine changes from **orange-brown to blue-black**, so **starch is present**.
**Negative result**: the iodine stays **orange-brown**, so **starch is absent**.
The deeper the blue-black colour, the more starch there is, but this is only a rough guide.
Foods that usually give a positive result include **bread, potato, rice and pasta**.
Iodine solution **stains skin and clothes** and is mildly harmful: wear eye protection and wipe up spills.
core.p: Starch is a carbohydrate made of many glucose molecules joined in long chains (a polysaccharide). **Iodine solution** is orange-brown, and it reacts with starch to form a **blue-black** colour. The test is quick, needs no heating, and is also the test used in the amylase practical because it can show whether starch is still present in a mixture at a given moment.

bullets: Place about **2 cm3 of food solution** in a test tube and add about **10 drops of Benedict's solution**.
Heat in a **water bath at about 75 degrees C** (or in hot water from a kettle) for about **5 minutes**. Use a water bath rather than a naked flame because it is safer and the temperature is steadier.
**Negative result**: the solution stays **blue**.
**Positive result**: the colour changes from blue to **green, yellow, orange or brick red**, depending on the amount of sugar.
The result is **semi-quantitative**: blue = none, green = trace or a little, yellow = some, orange = more, **brick red = a lot**.
Any change from blue shows that a sugar is present, so describe the change rather than just writing 'it changes colour'.
Foods that give a positive result include **fruit juice and sweet foods** (which contain glucose and fructose).
Hazards: Benedict's solution is an **irritant** and hot water can scald, so wear eye protection and use tongs or a holder.
core.p: **Benedict's solution** is a blue solution containing copper(II) ions. When it is heated with a **reducing sugar** such as glucose, the sugar reduces the copper(II) ions to give a coloured precipitate of copper(I) oxide, so the colour changes through green, yellow and orange to brick red. Heating is essential: without heat the reaction is far too slow to see.

bullets: Place about **2 cm3 of food solution** in a test tube.
Add **2 cm3 of sodium hydroxide solution** (or use ready-made **biuret reagent**) and mix.
Add a few **drops of dilute copper(II) sulfate solution** and shake gently.
**Positive result**: the solution turns from **blue to purple (lilac)**, so **protein is present**.
**Negative result**: the solution stays **blue**.
Foods that give a positive result include **egg white, meat, fish, milk and cheese**.
Hazards: **sodium hydroxide is corrosive**, so wear eye protection and tell the teacher about any spills; copper(II) sulfate is harmful.
core.p: Proteins are made of long chains of **amino acids**. The **biuret test** uses sodium hydroxide to make the mixture alkaline and then dilute copper(II) sulfate solution. Copper ions form a coloured complex with the peptide bonds that link amino acids, so a purple colour shows that protein is present. No heating is needed.

bullets: Place a small amount of the food (or **2 cm3 of food solution**) in a **dry** test tube.
Add about **2 cm3 of ethanol** and **shake thoroughly** so that any lipid dissolves.
Pour the ethanol mixture into a **second tube containing water**.
**Positive result**: a **cloudy white emulsion** forms, so **lipid is present**.
**Negative result**: the liquid stays **clear**.
The test tube must be dry at the start because water would stop the lipid dissolving in the ethanol.
Foods that give a positive result include **butter, oil, nuts and cheese**.
Hazards: **ethanol is highly flammable**, so keep it away from naked flames.
core.p: Lipids (fats and oils) do not dissolve in water but do dissolve in **ethanol**. In this test the lipid is first dissolved in ethanol, and when water is added, the lipid is no longer soluble and forms tiny droplets spread through the water. These droplets scatter light and make the liquid look **cloudy white**. This cloudy mixture is called an **emulsion**.

bullets: Always wear **eye protection** (goggles) because every reagent can irritate or damage the eyes.
Use **tongs or a test-tube holder** and a **water bath** for heating, and never point the open end of a tube at anyone.
Keep **ethanol** away from naked flames; heat Benedict's solution in a water bath, not over a Bunsen flame.
Use the **same volume of food solution and reagent** each time to make a fair comparison.

Include a **negative control** (distilled water plus reagent) to show what no reaction looks like, and a **positive control** (a known sample, such as glucose solution) to show what a positive looks like.
Compare colours against a **white background** or a colour chart to judge the result more objectively.
**Repeat** the test to check reproducibility, and clean equipment between tests to avoid **cross contamination**.
Do not taste any food or reagent in a laboratory.
core.h: Safety, controls and reliability in the food tests
core.p: Required practical questions regularly ask about hazards and about how to make results trustworthy. A **hazard** is something that could cause harm, a **risk** is the chance of that harm happening, and a **control** is the action you take to reduce the risk. You should be able to link each reagent to its hazard and a sensible precaution, and explain how to compare tests fairly.

bullets: **Specificity**: because the active site has a particular shape, each enzyme only works on one substrate (or a small group), which is why amylase does not break down proteins.
**Lock and key model**: the substrate is complementary in shape to the active site so it fits exactly.
Rate of reaction increases as temperature rises up to the **optimum**, because particles move faster, collide more often and with more energy.
Above the optimum temperature, or away from the optimum pH, the enzyme **denatures**: its shape changes and the active site no longer fits the substrate.
Denaturing is **permanent** for most enzymes: returning to the optimum conditions does not restore the shape.
Different enzymes have different optimum pH values. **Pepsin** in the stomach works best in acid (about pH 2), whereas **amylase** works best at around **pH 7** (neutral to slightly alkaline).
This practical links to the **digestive system**: amylase starts starch digestion in the mouth and continues in the small intestine.
core.h: Enzymes: the ideas behind the amylase practical
core.p: **Enzymes** are **biological catalysts**: they speed up reactions in living things without being used up. They are **proteins**, and each has an **active site** with a specific shape. The substrate fits the active site like a key fits a lock, forming an enzyme-substrate complex, and the reaction happens before the products leave. **Amylase** is a **carbohydrase** that breaks down **starch** into **maltose** (a sugar), and it is made in the salivary glands, the pancreas and the small intestine.

bullets: Put a **drop of iodine solution into each well** of a spotting tile (or into many wells in a row).

Place a **test tube of starch solution** and a **test tube of amylase solution** in a **water bath at a set temperature** (for example 30 to 35 degrees C) so that they reach the same temperature before mixing.
Add a measured volume of **buffer solution of a chosen pH** (for example pH 5) to the starch, then mix in the amylase and **start the stopwatch** immediately.
Every **30 seconds**, use a **dropping pipette (or glass rod)** to remove a drop of the mixture and add it to a fresh drop of iodine on the spotting tile.
Record the colour each time: **blue-black = starch still present**; **orange-brown = starch has all gone**.
Stop when the iodine stays **orange-brown**, and record the **time taken** for the starch to disappear.
**Repeat the whole investigation** with buffers of different pH values (for example pH 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9), keeping everything else the same.
**Repeat at each pH** (at least three times) and calculate a **mean** to improve reliability.
core.h: Required practical: investigating the effect of pH on amylase (method)
core.p: The aim is to find how **pH affects the rate at which amylase breaks down starch**. You mix amylase with starch at a fixed temperature and different pH values, using **buffer solutions** to hold each pH steady. At regular intervals you remove a drop of the mixture and add it to iodine solution. While starch is present the drop turns **blue-black**; when all the starch has been broken down the iodine stays **orange-brown**. The **time taken** for this to happen is measured.

bullets: **Independent variable**: the **pH** of the mixture, set using buffer solutions.
**Dependent variable**: the **time taken for starch to disappear** (when iodine stops turning blue-black), then converted to a rate.

**Control variables**: **temperature** (use a water bath and thermometer), **volume and concentration of amylase**, **volume and concentration of starch**, **volume of buffer**, and the **size of each drop** tested.
Temperature must be controlled because it also affects enzyme activity and would otherwise be a second variable.
Use the **same enzyme sample and the same stock of starch** for every pH.
Use a **fresh drop of iodine** each time, or the colour from earlier drops will interfere.
Keep the **time interval** the same (every 30 seconds) so that results are comparable.
core.h: Variables and control in the amylase practical
core.p: A fair test changes only one factor (the **independent variable**) and measures one outcome (the **dependent variable**), while every other factor is kept the same as **control variables**. Mark schemes often award marks for naming the variables, for saying how each is controlled, and for explaining why it needs to be controlled. If a control variable is not kept the same, you cannot be sure that the change in result was caused by the pH.

bullets: **Rate of reaction = 1 / time taken** (units: s-1). For example, 50 s gives 1/50 = **0.02 s-1**.
Using **1000 / time**: 50 s gives 1000/50 = **20** (arbitrary units).
Calculate the **mean time** from repeats before working out the rate, and **ignore anomalous results** in the mean (say that you have done this).
Plot **rate (y-axis) against pH (x-axis)** and draw a smooth **curve of best fit**, not straight lines joining the points.
The **peak of the curve** shows the **optimum pH**.
The rate is **zero (no reaction)** if iodine stays blue-black for the whole experiment, so the time is longer than you measured.
Always give an answer with **units** and to a sensible number of **significant figures**.
core.p: The investigation gives you a **time**, but the question is about **rate**. The shorter the time, the faster the reaction, so rate and time are **inversely proportional**. The usual calculation in the exam is rate = 1 / time, which gives units of **per second (s-1)**. Sometimes 1000 / time is used to give bigger numbers, which are easier to plot. Both are acceptable provided you use the same method for all the values.

bullets: At the **optimum pH** the enzyme works **fastest** because the shape of the active site is exactly complementary to the starch.
Moving away from the optimum, **hydrogen ions (H+) or hydroxide ions (OH-)** interfere with the **bonds that hold the enzyme in shape**.
The **active site changes shape**, so fewer substrate molecules fit, giving fewer enzyme-substrate complexes and a lower rate.
At **very low or very high pH** the active site is lost entirely and the enzyme is **denatured**, so no starch is broken down.
Describe a graph with **data**: for example 'the rate increases from 0.004 s-1 at pH 5 to a maximum of 0.017 s-1 at pH 7, then decreases'.
Compare enzymes: **pepsin** peaks at about pH 2, **amylase** about pH 7, **trypsin** about pH 8 to 9 (small intestine, alkaline conditions made by bile).
core.h: Interpreting the graph and the effect of pH
core.p: The graph of rate against pH is a **bell-shaped curve**. As pH moves towards the optimum, the rate rises to a **maximum** because the active site has its best shape. Beyond the optimum, the rate falls again. At extreme pH the enzyme is **denatured** and the rate is **zero**. Amylase has an optimum around **pH 7**, so the peak of the curve is near this value.

bullets: **Subjective end-point**: deciding when iodine stays orange-brown depends on the observer. A fix is to compare against a **colour standard**, or use a **colorimeter** to measure the colour objectively.
**Time interval**: sampling every 30 seconds means the true time could be up to 30 s earlier. Sampling **every 10 seconds** improves precision.
**Temperature drift**: keep tubes in a **water bath** with a thermometer, rather than standing them in the room.
**Mixing delay**: mix quickly and start the stopwatch at the instant the enzyme is added.
**Repeat and mean**: repeating at least three times shows whether results are **repeatable** and allows identification of **anomalies**.
**Wider range of pH** (for example pH 3 to 11) and **smaller steps** (for example every 0.5) will locate the optimum more accurately.
**Reproducible** results are those another scientist gets with a different method or equipment.
Buffers matter: without them, the pH would change as the reaction occurs, so the **independent variable** would not be controlled.
core.p: Evaluation questions ask you to comment on how **accurate, precise, repeatable or valid** the results are, and how to improve the method. Think about where errors come from, and what a better method could do. The method here has some weaknesses: judging when the colour is 'no longer blue-black' is subjective, and testing only every 30 seconds limits the precision of the time.

bullets: **Digestion**: amylase breaks starch to **maltose**; carbohydrase enzymes then break maltose to glucose. **Proteases** break down protein to amino acids and **lipases** break lipids to fatty acids and glycerol.
**Benedict's test** can be used on the amylase mixture: after digestion, the mixture gives a positive result for sugar, showing that the product has been made.
**Temperature version** of the practical: the same method, but keeping pH constant and changing the temperature of the water bath.
**Other enzyme practicals**: catalase and hydrogen peroxide, measuring the volume of oxygen collected over time.
**Industry**: enzymes are used in washing powders, in making **glucose syrup** from starch, and in **isomerase** to produce fructose syrup for sweeteners.
**Maths**: understand that **rate = change / time**, and compare rates using ratios or percentage change.
**Fair test language**: independent, dependent, control variable; hypothesis, prediction; accuracy, precision, repeatability, reproducibility, validity.
core.h: Links to other topics and Higher-tier thinking
core.p: This practical links across the specification. The same logic of designing a fair test, controlling variables and calculating a rate appears in the photosynthesis, osmosis and respiration practicals. In Higher-level questions you may be given unfamiliar data, such as an enzyme with a different optimum pH, and be asked to explain what the graph tells you. You apply the same reasoning each time: use the data, state the optimum, and explain the fall in rate in terms of **denaturation** and **active site shape**.

exam: **1-mark questions** usually ask for a colour change ('what colour shows starch?') or a reagent ('name the reagent used to test for protein'). Give the **start and end colours**: orange-brown to blue-black.
**2-mark questions** ask for a hazard and a precaution: name the hazard (for example 'ethanol is flammable') and give the matching precaution ('keep away from naked flames').

For a **4-mark method question on a food test**, give: sample preparation, reagent added, any heating (temperature and time), and the positive result colour. Use the sequence: prepare, add, heat if needed, observe.

For the **amylase practical (6 marks)** include: temperature control in a **water bath**, **buffers** of different pH, mixing and starting a **stopwatch**, **samples every 30 s onto iodine**, the **end-point** (orange-brown), **repeats** and a **mean**.
When asked for **variables**, name them and state how each is controlled: 'temperature was kept at 30 degrees C using a water bath'.
**Rate calculations**: write the formula, substitute with numbers, then give the answer with units (s-1). Show working because method marks are available.
**Graph questions**: 'describe' means state the trend using data from the graph with units; 'explain' means give the reason, using **active site, shape, denatured, complementary**.

For **'explain why the rate decreased at pH 9'** write: the pH is away from the optimum; the bonds holding the enzyme in shape are affected; the **active site changes shape**; fewer substrates fit; fewer enzyme-substrate complexes form.
**Evaluation** answers need a **problem plus a solution**: 'colour change is subjective, so use a colorimeter' scores; 'it was not accurate' does not.
Use **command word** guidance: **describe** (what happens), **explain** (why, with reasoning), **evaluate** (strengths, weaknesses and a conclusion), **suggest** (apply knowledge to a new case).
Always link the **dependent variable to the reason**: faster rate means shorter time for starch to disappear.

mistakes.r: Iodine goes from orange-brown to blue-black when starch is present; it stays orange-brown when starch is absent.
mistakes.w: Iodine turns clear / goes brown when starch is present.

mistakes.r: Benedict's must be heated in a hot water bath; it then goes from blue to green, yellow, orange or brick red.
mistakes.w: Benedict's turns red when you add it.

mistakes.r: A positive protein result is blue to purple (lilac); a negative result stays blue.
mistakes.w: Biuret test: the solution turns purple if it is negative.

mistakes.r: Dissolve in ethanol, then add water; a cloudy white emulsion shows lipid is present.
mistakes.w: The ethanol test: it turns white if lipids are present, with no mention of water.

mistakes.r: Enzymes are not alive; they are denatured, meaning the shape of the active site is changed so the substrate no longer fits.
mistakes.w: Enzymes are killed by high temperature or extreme pH.

mistakes.r: Enzymes are catalysts and are not used up; they can be used again.
mistakes.w: The enzyme is used up in the reaction.

mistakes.r: Rate = 1 / time, so a shorter time means a faster rate.
In the pH practical, pH is the independent variable; temperature and volumes are the control variables.
Use a water bath at about 75 degrees C, because it is safer and controls the temperature.
mistakes.w: Use a Bunsen burner flame to heat Benedict's test tubes.

summary: You must use iodine, Benedict's, biuret and ethanol emulsion tests to identify starch, sugars, protein and lipids, and investigate how pH affects the rate at which amylase breaks down starch. It matters because these are required practicals, tested with method, calculation, graph and evaluation questions.

terms.d: A test that tells you whether a substance is present from a change such as colour, without measuring how much.
A chemical solution used in a test to detect a substance by producing a visible change.
Orange-brown reagent that turns blue-black in the presence of starch.
Blue reagent that, on heating with a reducing sugar, changes to green, yellow, orange or brick red.
Alkaline copper(II) sulfate solution that turns from blue to purple when protein is present.
A cloudy white mixture of tiny droplets of one liquid (such as lipid) spread through another (water).
A carbohydrate made of many glucose molecules joined together, stored by plants.
A sugar, such as glucose, that reduces Benedict's solution to give a coloured precipitate.
A biological catalyst, made of protein, that speeds up a specific reaction without being used up.
The part of an enzyme with a specific shape where the substrate binds.
The molecule that an enzyme acts on, which fits the active site.
When the shape of an enzyme (and its active site) is permanently changed so it can no longer bind the substrate.
The pH at which an enzyme works fastest.
A solution that resists changes in pH, used to keep the pH constant.
A carbohydrase enzyme that breaks down starch into maltose.
The variable that the investigator deliberately changes.
The variable that is measured as the outcome.
A variable that is kept the same so that the test is fair.
Something that has the potential to cause harm.
A result that does not fit the pattern and is outside the range of the other repeat results.

worked.ans: Add sodium hydroxide solution to the food solution, then add a few drops of copper(II) sulfate solution. If protein is present, the colour changes from blue to purple (lilac). If there is no protein, it stays blue.
worked.q: A student tests a food for protein. Describe how the student should carry out the test and what result shows protein is present. (3 marks)
steps: Prepare the food solution: grind the food with distilled water and filter if needed.
Add sodium hydroxide solution (or biuret reagent) to the food solution in a test tube.
Add a few drops of dilute copper(II) sulfate solution and mix.

worked.ans: Rate at pH 7 = 0.0167 s-1 (1/60). It is 4 times faster than at pH 5.
worked.q: A student measures the time for amylase to break down all the starch at three pH values: pH 5 took 240 s, pH 7 took 60 s, pH 9 took 400 s. Calculate the rate (1/time) at pH 7 and state how many times faster this is than at pH 5. (3 marks)
steps: At pH 7: rate = 1 / 60 = 0.0167 s-1 (to 3 significant figures).

worked.ans: pH 7 is near the optimum pH for amylase. At pH 9 the pH changes the bonds holding the protein in shape, so the shape of the active site changes (the enzyme starts to denature). The starch is no longer a complementary fit, so fewer enzyme-substrate complexes form, and starch is broken down more slowly.
worked.q: Explain why the rate of reaction of amylase is lower at pH 9 than at pH 7. (4 marks)
steps: State that pH 7 is near the optimum and pH 9 is away from it.
Say that the pH change affects the bonds holding the enzyme in shape.
Say that the shape of the active site changes (denatured).
Say that the substrate no longer fits, so fewer enzyme-substrate complexes form.
